chapter_theme: The second half of the neythal kali of Nallanthuvanar: two friend's pleas to a lord of the shore built on refrains and on the dice game (135, 136), a heroine's night lament (137), four madal poems in which the man rides the palm horse and sings to the town and its worthies (138 to 141), six poems of a woman whose love has unhinged her, singing to onlookers, sun, moon and sea until her lover comes back (142 to 147), the evening lament (148), a friend's argument for marriage from gratitude and oath (149) and a paalai consolation set in Shiva's images (150).

135.reading: The friend tells the lord of the shore, where the wave, with paired conches for tusks and the wind for its mahout, charges the high dune at midnight like a war elephant at a fort gate, that if he abandons the girl who lost her beauty to him under the punnai, her bangles slipping, her body sick and her flower eyes scorned, it will lie as a great fault on his lineage, a deceit on his truthfulness and a blemish on his fame; if he has heard her, let him drive his tall chariot quickly to her, the gem chain swinging on his chest.
135.nuance: The triple refrain sets three losses of hers (beauty, health, the bloom of her eyes) against three goods of his (குடிமை, வாய்மை, புகழ்மை), so her body becomes the ledger of his honour. The wave that rams the dune at midnight like an elephant at a fort may hint at the man's night visits, but only one correspondence maps, so it is left as a simile, not ullurai.

thinai_evidence.note: conch, wave and punnai of the shore, with the shore lord addressed

comparisons.vehicle: இணை திரள் மருப்பு ஆக எறி வளி பாகனா
comparisons.tenor: the paired conches as the wave's tusks and the wind as its driver

iraicchi.act: the conch rises on the wave joined with its mate (துணை புணர்ந்து)
iraicchi.sense: even the conch of his own sea keeps to its partner, so a lord of this shore who leaves the woman he joined falls below the creatures of his shore

136.reading: The friend tells the lord of the lovely sea, where crabs dance in burrows that the waves have scored like the marks dice leave on the gaming floor, that each time he was kind to the girl on the pearl-white dune, in the bent screwpine's thicket and under the punnai she swelled like a gambler whose throw comes up winning, and asks whether, now he means to leave, she must suffer like the one who lost by the stake or the traveller who strayed and lost his bundle; let him not fear the gossip, take her by the rightful way so that her beauty gathers greater than the wealth of the Pandya king, and mount the chariot.
136.nuance: The whole poem is built on the dice game the opening scene supplies: the gaming words (பத்து, வித்தம், வித்தாயம், மறு வித்தம், சிறு வித்தம்) name throws and stakes whose exact values are not recoverable, but the pattern is clear, each meeting place a winning throw and each leaving a lost stake, so the friend turns his kindness into a gamble he must end by marriage.

thinai_evidence.note: crab, screwpine, punnai and boats of the shore

comparisons.tenor: the crab's scored burrows in the sand
the white sand of the dune
her gladness when he is kind
her loss when he strays from the right way

137.reading: The woman tells her friend that holding to modesty is hard, love is great and her life very small, the night watches are many and full of sorrow, and only the andril birds keep her company; trembling like a peacock losing its beauty, she finds her bed turned to fire, the fruit of his smile; he struck her only with words, not with a bow, yet the sickness born of his words is harsher than the bow; he hurt her only through the grace of friendship, not through old enmity, yet that is harsher than enmity; he burned her only with his gentleness, not with fire, yet that burns worse than fire; if such lovers are the physicians who could give back her life, what will become of her? unless she can hold firm, the sickness he gave will not leave.
137.nuance: The three refrains each concede a milder weapon (word, friendship, gentleness) and then rank its wound above the harsher one (bow, enmity, fire), so the poem argues that love's injuries are worse because they come from kindness. The andril, the bird that will not part from its mate, keeps her company only by calling through the night; it carries a mood, not an act, and is left as scene. The last two lines turn on வலித்தன்று and can also be read as a resolve to endure.

thinai_evidence.note: the andril calling through the night watches

comparisons.tenor: the sickness born of his words
the lovers who alone could cure her

138.reading: The man says that as the goad straightens and fails in the mahout's hand when the elephant's must flows, so his knowledge, restraint and shame have gone and others laugh at him, for she who showed her form like the flicker of lightning or a dream has carried off his heart and hidden her beauty; tying peacock feathers, pulai, avirai and erukku to his horse, he sings in the street of the rich town: grief and the palmyra-born horse are what she gave, and his life will dissolve like a salt doll in rain; pulai and golden avirai are the flowers she gave, and his life will melt like wax in fire; only the young and strangers ask after him; hearing the song she came with loving words and grace, and she pitied the madal, his companion in suffering, which would have no place in his joy now that he had her, as those who strive in hard penance leave their bodies behind when they reach the high world.
138.nuance: She gives two things in the refrains, grief together with the madal and the madal's flowers, so the instrument of his public shame is counted as her gift. The close is unexpected: she pities the madal, which served him in sorrow and must now be discarded, and the simile of ascetics leaving their bodies makes the palm-stem horse the body of his penance.

thinai_evidence.note: the man who rides the palmyra-stem horse for a woman (ஏறிய மடல் திறம்)

comparisons.tenor: the man's restraint failing before his desire

comparisons.vehicle: உப்பு இயல் பாவை உறை உற்றது போல
அரும் தவம் முயன்றோர் தம் உடம்பு ஒழித்து உயர் உலகு இனிது பெற்றாங்கே
comparisons.tenor: the madal left behind once he gains her

139.reading: The man tells the worthies of the assembly that since it is the duty of the worthy to guard others' pain as their own and to know what is right, he will inform them: a woman appeared to him like lightning among rain drops, showed him her form and took his heart, so he cannot sleep; crowned with a garland of avirai and erukku, bells ringing, he rides the stem of the tall palmyra and sings of her; tossed night and day by waves of grief in the sea of love she caused without feeling it, he swims with the madal as his raft; the horse she gave is the cure for a sickness past cure, the shelter against the army that Kama sends to break his manly beauty, and the shade against love's fire; so, as the sages raised again to the high world the king who had fallen from heaven, it is their duty to end his distress.
139.nuance: He frames the madal as a petition: the opening and closing lines put the duty on the worthies (சான்றீர்), and the three refrains call the horse a cure, a shelter and a shade, the very things the assembly should give. The king fallen from heaven and restored by sages is an epic story the poet assumes; the name is not given.

thinai_evidence.note: the madal rider pleading before the assembly (ஏறிய மடல் திறம்)

comparisons.tenor: the madal that carries him through love

comparisons.vehicle: அரசனைப் பெயர்த்து அவர் உயர்நிலை உலகம் உறீஇயாங்கு

140.reading: The man tells the people who rush up and stare as if they had never seen the like that what he rides is a horse, not a palm stem, and these are no mere flowers but a garland of pulai and ulinjai, peacock feathers from the hill field, bells on a thread and an avirai chaplet like beaten gold, given as if by the son of the Tall One; he goes to show his servitude to a woman of finished beauty whose gentleness breaks his heart; he can sing if told to sing and dance if told to dance, and offers to sing the horse she gave as a cure; the worthy show their love even when they cannot free the moon from the snake, a snake that kills in rage may be spared if caught by an assembly, a man in a whirlpool can breathe when those on the bank say 'fear not', but this town sees his sickness and knows his love and does not soften; if they look clearly and make her grant him grace, the virtue will be theirs.
140.nuance: The three refrains each set a case where onlookers help though they cannot cure (the eclipse, the snake, the drowning boy) against the town that sees, knows and does nothing (கண்டும் கண்ணோடாது); the madal is an appeal to the town's கண்ணோட்டம, and the closing line makes granting it an act of அறம்.

thinai_evidence.note: the madal rider shows himself to the town (ஏறிய மடல் திறம்)

comparisons.tenor: the garland worn as a lover's gift
the town's indifference to his sickness

comparisons.vehicle: வெம் சுழிப் பட்ட மகற்குக் கரை நின்றார் அஞ்சல் என்றாலும்
comparisons.tenor: the comfort the town could give him

141.reading: The man tells the worthies that the learned have declared riding the palm-stem horse and singing a woman's beauty to be among the acts of those who, born in a body hard to gain, reach none of the three ends of virtue, wealth and pleasure; yet she, close at times yet as hard to grasp as the full moon's image in water, made him, who rides the war horse in battle, go to the common on the madal horse; she wants the spotless disk on the banner of the truthful world, and made him, whose heart was set on protecting the earth, eager to beg; she seemed to want to seize the lightning that splits the night, and made him, who could speak before the sharpest tongues, show himself unlettered before others; as he rode in pain through the street and sang words fitting her, her kin gave her to him as enemies give hard tribute to Vazhuthi, mighty in war.
141.nuance: Each refrain sets a reversal of rank: the war horse becomes the madal horse, the protector of the earth a beggar, the eloquent man a dunce; the opening concedes that the learned rank madal outside all three ends of life, so the plea is made against the code it cites. Lines 11 and 12 (the disk on the banner of the truthful world) are obscure, and the reading of that refrain is not settled.

thinai_evidence.note: the madal rider pleads before the worthies (ஏறிய மடல் திறம்)

comparisons.tenor: her kin giving her to him

142.reading: The poet says that love which, short of union, keeps one lover far is more fruitless than a lute whose string has snapped, and shows a girl who once smiled with hidden teeth among her friends now laughing aloud so that all hear and then weeping; she sings to the onlookers: would they laugh if she could embrace the deceiver's chest? if she had the strength to say 'he ruined me', would her neythal eyes have paled? she would catch the crescent moon and hide it in her little house, and would Shiva then wander looking for it? will he come back, or will she sit and scorn him? in a dream she seized him and he vanished from her hand as she woke; she asks the setting sun to put him in her outstretched hand, and to lend her a few rays as a lamp to search for him; she tells the mango shoot on the palmyra of the common that she sees nothing good or bad but his grace; her tears would burn the world if she let them fall; she begs the worthies to remove love and gossip, the two pains that hang her life; then the husband who had given her nights of grace came, and she grew clear and well again, like muddy water cleared with clearing-nut, leaning on his breast.
142.nuance: Her speech moves from argument (would you laugh if I had him?) to fantasy (she would steal Shiva's crescent and he would wander for it) to appeals to the sun, a mango shoot and the worthies; the dream in which he vanishes from her hand on waking (lines 33 to 36) is the hinge. The two closing similes, water clearing in a gem and muddy water cleared by the nut, make her madness a clouding that his return settles.

thinai_evidence.note: a woman whose love has passed beyond restraint into public lament (தேறுதல் ஒழிந்த காமம்)

comparisons.tenor: love that stops short of union

143.reading: The woman tells the onlookers, who ask what has happened to her, dulled like the moon by day, her tilakam gone, pallor covering her as if gold had been laid on her or kanikaram flowers whirled on mango shoots, that a man left her as openly as a drum proclaims, crueller than one who heard a deer drawn by his lute and killed it on the rock, and her heart has gone far after him; if they bring him she will regain her restraint; let them not fret, for her life shows him safe; she has come to beg the blameless sun, who scorches the unjust, not to leave her out when it punishes him; the town sings wearing mango shoots, and she would flower if he returned; he is skilled at braiding neythal, drawing cane on her shoulders and tholil on her breasts; evening has come like death, the backwater flowers closing like her thoughts, the herders' flute sounding like her grieving heart, the lute fading like her voice and the day vanishing like her lustre; the sun sets without her, gossip spreads, her eyes, once blue lilies to him, are pale as peerkku flowers; why does the king who guards all lives as his own not guard hers? then the man who had crossed many hills came humbly to her feet, and she regained her smile and her lost beauty like the land the Pandya made calm.
143.nuance: The evening passage (lines 36 to 41) inverts the usual simile: the landscape is compared to her (the flowers close like her thought, the flute sounds like her heart), so the scene is read as the copy and her grief as the original. Her last appeal turns the puram ideal of the king who guards every life as his own against him, since he cannot guard hers. Lines 10 to 13 (the deer drawn by the lute and the land called அறை நவ நாடு) are obscure.

thinai_evidence.note: a deserted wife whose grief has passed into bewilderment (தேறுதல் ஒழிந்த காமம்)

comparisons.vehicle: நினையும் என் உள்ளம் போல் நெடும் கழி மலர் கூம்ப
comparisons.tenor: the closing of the backwater flowers

comparisons.vehicle: இனையும் என் நெஞ்சம் போல் இனம் காப்பார் குழல் தோன்ற

144.reading: Someone points out to a companion a girl who sighs, laughs, weeps without wiping her tears, stares at the ground and answers strangely, and they go to hear her; she says a man who swore his life hung on telling her his pain fed her love and changed, and she will search everywhere for him: she asks the hare in the moon, who sees the whole sea, to show where he is, or she will set fierce dogs on it, tell the hunters, and have the snake swallow it with the moon; when a cloud covers the moon she thinks it pities her; she will run through the screwpine groves and show where he made her garland of adumbu flowers, where he ran off with her doll, where he drew tholil on her, where he embraced her saying 'be consoled'; she asks the wind to find the one who ate her beauty and hid, or she will burn the earth with her tears, and threatens to bail the sea dry; she hates day and night alike; when she opens her eyes to catch him he runs and hides in her heart; love's fire burns even in water; had she known she would not have embraced him; then her lover came quickly and her pallor vanished like slander against a just man before a good assembly.
144.nuance: Her threats to the moon, the wind and the sea are a child's threats (dogs for the hare, the snake for the moon, bailing the sea), and the places she points out are those of a childhood game (the doll he ran off with), so her madness returns her to the age of the first meeting. Lines 55 to 58 make the waking lover flee into her heart, the one place she cannot search.

thinai_evidence.note: a woman whose love has unhinged her, addressing moon, wind and sea (தேறுதல் ஒழிந்த காமம்)

comparisons.tenor: her wavering between sense and confusion
love's fire set against a fire that water quenches
virtue as the raft that may carry her effort

comparisons.vehicle: திறன் இலார் எடுத்து தீ மொழி எல்லாம் நல் அவைஉள் படக் கெட்டாங்கு

145.reading: The woman tells the townspeople, who laugh that love is like a dream that gives nothing in waking and that she wanders, weeps for the man who enjoyed and left her and then laughs as if she had forgotten him, not to laugh: that men leave the women they embraced and those gone over long wastes come quickly back is a turn, like night and day, that comes to all who live; she asks the cloud why it roars dry over his forest instead of drawing rain from the sea of her tears; the fierce day seems to foment her sickness; she begs the sun not to set, for evening will kill her, and asks whether she could bear the enmity of evening and its dew if he came over the sea at dawn; when the sea dims, the shore grows lonely and the neythal closes under the moon, she asks whether the one she wants sleeps with the one he wants, while her heart searches sky and earth; she asks the moon to go to him; the townspeople cured her love with rites, but her husband would not scorn her however they mock; let the dark sky rain on her, for the fire has caught all over; then those who sought him brought him as virtue answers a just complaint, she joined him like Sri on Vishnu's chest, and her grief vanished like darkness before the sun.
145.nuance: She answers the town's mockery with a general law (leaving and returning alternate like night and day for everyone), so her lament claims to be ordinary experience, not madness. The townspeople's rites to cure her (வினைக் கொண்டு, line 51) are the veri the akam heroine usually suffers at her mother's hands, here taken over by the town.

thinai_evidence.note: a deserted wife whose grief has passed into bewilderment (தேறுதல் ஒழிந்த காமம்)

comparisons.tenor: love as the onlookers see it
the people who brought her husband back

146.reading: The poet says that love, which raises those who join it high and then drops them into trouble without bound, is more pitiless than a king who rules by punishment, and shows a girl, left by the man who loved her on a swan-soft bed, standing on the chariot road, shame and restraint forgotten, tears running over her breasts; she tells those who ask whether she has lost her shame that the sickness he left on her is like a sky that ended a drought and like a flood that fills and drowns her; she has not lost her shame, beauty and heart, for they stayed with him; she laughed with the red-spotted crab, remembering; he who will marry her will not leave her; she told the sun to search the sea-girt world and will go wherever she hears of him; if evening and midnight come she will sing her pain among the crowd, and the night that sends all to sleep would not sleep if it heard her; she tells the sleeping worthies of the town to dam the water, for even the rains would not cool her; staying, her heart burns, going, her body suffers, so she will go like a jointed doll; hearing her, he came, and as rain pours on the bird that cries for drops in a dry sky, his embrace ended her distress.
146.nuance: She denies the charge of shamelessness with a paradox: her shame, beauty and heart are not lost but left with him, so what the town sees is only the body without them. Her threat to the night (lines 36 to 41) is that her song would keep even the night awake and make the moon tremble.

thinai_evidence.note: a woman who has passed beyond shame in her longing (தேறுதல் ஒழிந்த காமம்)

comparisons.tenor: the sickness that settled on her

147.reading: The poet asks whether love has become like the stupor of those who drink strong toddy, and shows a girl who once walked with ringing anklets now in the street as if she had lost the man who ate her beauty, without food, without the shame dearer than life, laughing and then weeping; she asks who these staring people are, says her heart was caught in the net of a man who did not know the worth of her eyes, brows, shoulders, waist and cloud-dark hair, and that he who calmed her with oaths embraced her and left, the killer; she asks the sun to show where he is or else what use is it in the sky, warns it of being devoured where it appears in water like the moon, and asks whether he has gone past the forest of unmilked buffaloes or stays in this town doing wrong; she asks Kama, king of the shark banner, to write down his cruelty, and asks whether his arrows torment all who love one man; if she sees him she will look softly, seize his cloth and cry 'thief!' if he pretends not to know her; his bond has joined her life like drink and made her eyes sleepless; if the sun will not show him she will clasp Kama's feet and beg his arrows so that he comes riding the palmyra horse; then, like the swan joining his mate as she hurries to him, she saw her lover come, forgot her grief and leaned shyly on his breast.
147.nuance: The madal is turned around at the close: the woman does not ride it but begs Kama's arrows so that the man will ride it to her (lines 59, 60), keeping the convention that a woman does not mount the palm horse while making her the cause of his mounting. Lines 32 and 36 to 38 (the toad that eats the sun, the kite's eye, the forest of unmilked buffaloes) are obscure.

thinai_evidence.note: a woman whose love has driven her into the street (தேறுதல் ஒழிந்த காமம்)

148.reading: The woman tells the evening that it has come and camped outside her departing life, as the sun, its work in the old world done, goes to the hill like one who has carried out the task his master set, the moon combs the dark over the waves like the gracious face of one who destroys wrong, and the backwater flowers close like the conduct of the poor; she charges it that while it is a sweet suggestion to the happy and inflames the love of the united, it torments those left in tears and terrifies the deserted; it neither brings her husband nor keeps her company, a sickness to the parted and a raft to the joined; then, to end her grief, as day clears the spreading dark, her far-dwelling lover returned, his task done, having seized his enemies' land.
148.nuance: Line 9 uses the word இறைச்சி itself: the evening is the suggestive setting (இறைச்சி) for the happy, so the poem names the device by which a time of day carries love's sense and then complains that the same hour means the opposite to the parted. The three similes of sunset (a servant done with work, a just ruler's face, the conduct of the poor) all come from the life of the town and the state.

thinai_evidence.note: evening on the backwaters, the hour and land of neythal (porul 1.10)

comparisons.vehicle: வல்லவன் கூறிய வினை தலை வைத்தான் போல்
comparisons.tenor: the sun going down its work done

comparisons.vehicle: அல்லது கெடுப்பவன் அருள் கொண்ட முகம் போல
comparisons.tenor: the moon rising over the waves

comparisons.vehicle: பாய் இருள் பரப்பினை பகல் களைந்தது போலப்
comparisons.tenor: her grief ended by his return

149.reading: The friend tells the lord of the shore, whose sea surges like a king on the march with rows of boats for elephants, the roar of waves for drums and the wings of the shore birds for his army, that her beauty wastes alone like the learning of a pupil who grieves his teacher and will not share, and like wealth hoarded while kin grieve in a family without effort; that failing those who helped one in want will strike the doer even in his descendants, and that a man who breaks the deed he swore will not be spared, however good his sword; let him think of her state, for she suffers with a racing heart like the distress of a town when an angry king camps outside its walls.
149.nuance: The friend argues entirely in the language of puram and ethics (the ungrateful pupil, the hoarding family, the oath-breaker, the besieged town), so the case for marriage is put as a duty of gratitude and of keeping one's sworn word (சூள்), not as a plea of love. The sea pictured as a king on the march frames the man as the conqueror besieging her.

thinai_evidence.note: boats, waves and shore birds of the sea coast

comparisons.vehicle: நிரை திமில் களிறு ஆகத் திரை ஒலி பறை ஆக
comparisons.tenor: the boats and the roar of the sea as the king's elephants and drums

comparisons.vehicle: எயில் புறத்து இறுத்த வினை வரு பருவரல் போல

150.reading: The friend tells the woman that those who left her for gain, giving up virtue, to cross the hot waste where a bamboo fire, kindled by the sun like the fire born when Shiva of the konrai garland shot the moving forts, spreads roaring over the hill, confuses the paths and leaps to the sky, will not abandon her while her colour, like the ornament of the god who hid the river in his hair, turns pale; those who left for great wealth, not calling the road fearful, will remember her as her form fades; those who left for bright wealth, not calling the path impassable, will see her as her hair dries; and so, like the great champak that bloomed in full to adorn the lord of the Ardra star, they are sure he will not prove false.
150.nuance: Every simile comes from Shiva (the burning of the forts, the river in his hair, the bull-rider's ornament, the crescent chaplet, the Ardra star), so the friend's comfort is set in a frame of worship. She concedes that he left 'giving up virtue' (அறம் துறந்து) and still holds that he will not be false, separating his breach of virtue from his keeping of his word. The colophon files it under neythal, but nothing of the shore is in it.

thinai_evidence.note: the man has left for wealth across a burning waste

comparisons.vehicle: இயங்கு எயில் எயப் பிறந்த எரி போல
comparisons.tenor: the forest fire on the hill

comparisons.vehicle: சடைக் கரந்தான் அணி அன்ன நின் நிறம்

comparisons.tenor: the certainty of his keeping faith

links.note: Kalittokai 135's friend tells the shore lord that abandoning the girl would lie as a great fault on his lineage (குடிமைக் கண் பெரியது ஓர் குற்றம்); Kural 957 says a fault in the well-born stands out high like the spot on the moon.
links.teaches: The couplet's rule that high birth makes a fault more visible is what gives the friend's threat its force: she aims at his lineage rather than his love because a lord's desertion, unlike a commoner's, would be seen by all, so the maxim is already a working argument in akam persuasion.

links.note: Kalittokai 136 likens the girl's joy at each meeting to a gambler's winning throw and her grief at his leaving to the loss of a stake; Kural 932 says the gambler gains one and loses a hundred.
links.teaches: Read with the couplet's arithmetic of the dice, the friend's simile becomes a warning: a secret love that runs on wins and losses must end in ruin on balance, which is why she ends by telling him to take the girl in marriage and stop the game.

links.note: Kalittokai 137 says his gentleness burns her worse than fire (தீயினும் கடிது); Kural 1159 says fire burns only when touched, while love's sickness burns when the lover is away.
links.teaches: The couplet states as a single paradox what the kali poem reaches through three graded steps (word above bow, kindness above enmity, gentleness above fire), so the Kural's compressed contrast between fire and love was the end point of an argued rhetoric the longer form still displays.

links.note: Kalittokai 138's madal rider sings that grief and the palmyra horse are what she gave (படரும் பனை ஈன்ற மாவும் நல்கியவை); in Kural 1135 the man says the girl gave him the madal and evening's anguish.
links.teaches: Both men list the madal among the woman's gifts, so the convention made the beloved the author of the lover's public shame; the kali poem adds the outcome the couplet leaves open, her coming in grace, which shows the gift was meant to be returned.

links.note: Kalittokai 139 calls the horse she gave a shelter (ஏமம்) against the army of love; Kural 1131 says that for those who suffer in love there is no safeguard (ஏமம்) and no strength but the madal.
links.teaches: Both use the same word ஏமம் for an act of humiliation, and the kali poem shows how the safeguard works: it is spoken to the worthies whose duty is to treat another's pain as their own, so the madal protects by putting the assembly under obligation.

links.note: Kalittokai 139's rider swims the sea of love with the madal as his raft (மடல் புணையா நீந்துவேன்); Kural 1134 says the fierce flood of love carries off the raft of shame and manliness.
links.teaches: Where the couplet's flood sweeps away the raft of shame, the kali lover takes the shameful act itself as his raft, so the two together show the madal as what is left when shame has failed: a raft made of the loss of one.

links.note: Kalittokai 140's rider complains that the town sees his sickness and does not soften (கண்டும் கண்ணோடாது இவ் ஊர்); Kural 576 says those who have eyes and do not turn them kindly are like trees fixed in the soil.
links.teaches: The madal rider appeals to the civic virtue the Kural names கண்ணோட்டம், so the madal is shown to work through the town's duty of kindly regard, and the town that will not soften is, by the Kural's measure, as insensible as a tree.

links.note: Kalittokai 141's rider says she made him, who rides the war horse in battle, ride the madal to the common; in Kural 1133 the man says he once had shame and manliness and now has the madal.
links.teaches: The couplet's before-and-after inventory is spelled out in the kali poem as three lost ranks (warrior, protector, orator), which shows that the manliness the Kural says is lost is a public standing, not only a private virtue.

links.note: Kalittokai 142's girl, once laughing with hidden teeth, now laughs aloud and weeps so all hear and sings her love to the worthies; Kural 1138 says love does not stop to weigh restraint but breaks secrecy and comes into the open.
links.teaches: The couplet states as a law what the kali poem stages as a scene with an audience and a song, and shows the price: once love breaks into the open, the woman faces two pains, love and gossip (காமமும் கௌவையும்), where the couplet names only the first.

links.note: Kalittokai 143's woman asks why the king who guards the world's lives as his own does not guard hers; Purananuru 186 says the world lives by its king and the king must know he is its life.
links.teaches: The deserted woman takes the puram doctrine that the king is the people's life and finds its edge: a king can guard every life from war and want but not from a lover's leaving, so the akam poem marks a limit of royal protection that the puram counsel does not state.

links.note: Kalittokai 144's girl says that when she opens her eyes to seize him he runs and hides in her heart; Kural 1218 says that when she sleeps he is on her shoulder and when she wakes he quickly moves into her heart.
links.teaches: The same fancy of the lover fleeing into the heart on waking appears in both, but the kali poem frames it as a madwoman's complaint to the sea, so what the couplet offers as consolation (he never leaves her) is also a sign of her derangement.

links.note: Kalittokai 145's woman begs the sun not to set and speaks of bearing evening's enmity (மாலைப் பகை); Kural 1225 asks what good she did to morning and what enmity (பகை) to evening.
links.teaches: The couplet's riddle about why evening is hostile is answered in the kali poem by an action: she asks the sun to stay and hopes the man will come at dawn over the sea, so the hours are enemies or friends according to when the parted can expect his return.

links.note: Kalittokai 146's woman says that if she told her pain to the night that puts many to sleep (பலர்த் துயிற்றும் யாமம்), it would not sleep; Kural 1168 says the night that puts all beings to sleep has no companion but her.
links.teaches: Both make the night, the one who puts all to sleep, the only wakeful companion of the deserted woman; the kali poem goes further and threatens to keep the night itself awake with her song, turning the couplet's pity for the night into her power over it.

links.note: Kural 1137 says nothing is worthier than womanhood that suffers a sea of desire and does not ride the madal; Kalittokai 147's woman, maddened in the street, begs Kama's arrows so that the man will come riding the palmyra horse.
links.teaches: The kali woman keeps the rule the couplet praises, she does not mount the madal, but she gets around it by wishing the madal on him, so the restriction on women survives even in the most extreme akam scene and shapes the form her desire takes.

links.note: Kalittokai 148 calls evening a sickness to the parted and a raft to the joined; in Kural 1226 the woman did not know evening brings sickness while her husband was still with her.
links.teaches: The couplet records the discovery and the kali poem the double nature behind it: the same hour is a raft and a suggestive setting (இறைச்சி) for lovers together and a sickness for the parted, which is why she learned its cruelty only after he left.

links.note: Kalittokai 149's friend warns that failing those who helped in want will strike the doer even in his descendants; Kural 110 says one who kills a good done to him has no escape.
links.teaches: The friend applies the Kural's gravest moral rule to a lover's delay, so the woman who gave herself in secret is counted as a benefactor, and his failure to marry her becomes ingratitude, the one wrong with no escape.

links.note: Purananuru 34 quotes dharma that there is expiation for many crimes but none for those who kill a benefit; Kalittokai 149's friend says ingratitude to helpers will not spare a man, however good his sword.
links.teaches: The rule the puram poet uses to praise a king's gifts to bards is turned in the akam poem against a lover, which shows the ethic of gratitude ran across both halves of Sangam poetry and could bind a man's private love as tightly as a patron's duty.

links.note: In Kalittokai 16 virtue itself runs to block the man's venture for wealth; in Kalittokai 150 the friend says he left 'giving up virtue' (அறம் துறந்து) and still assures the woman that he will not prove false.
links.teaches: In 16 virtue is the force that keeps him home, while in 150 the friend grants that he broke virtue by going and yet trusts his word, so the two poems split the man's duty into staying (அறம்) and keeping faith (not being பொய்), which can come apart.

source_issues: kalittokai 135-150: the core records give the poet as நல்லாந்துவனார் for every poem; the neythal kali is usually ascribed to நல்லந்துவனார், and the spelling may be a variant or a misprint (recorded, not corrected).

kalittokai 135-150: the colophon gives neythal for all sixteen; 138-147 are madal and unrestrained-love poems (perunthinai: ஏறிய மடல் திறம் and தேறுதல் ஒழிந்த காமம்), and 150 is a paalai poem of leaving for wealth with nothing of the shore in it.
kalittokai 135-150: no colophon thurai, so thurai_akam speaker, addressee and stage are inferred and occasion.words is null.
kalittokai:138, 141, 143, 144, 146, 149: ஃ restored from the old encoding (flag repaired).
kalittokai:145 line 1: a damaged word was replaced by the sangamtamil.com reading (flag repaired); the sense (those who hasten, துனையுநர்) fits the line.
kalittokai:144 line 8 and kalittokai:146 line 10: the same line (கூறுப கேளாமோ, சென்று) is flagged as repeated; it is a formula of the narrator in these poems, not a copying error.
kalittokai:141 lines 11-12, kalittokai:143 lines 10-13, kalittokai:147 lines 32 and 36-38: obscure lines; readings marked uncertain.
